questions.prompt: Which appliances use the heating effect of current? Choose all that apply.
questions.explain: A fan uses the magnetic effect in its motor.

questions.prompt: Why are heating coils made of nichrome, not copper?
options: Nichrome has a high resistance and a high melting point, so it gets very hot without melting
questions.explain: High resistance produces lots of heat; a high melting point stops it melting.

questions.prompt: How does a fuse protect a circuit?
options: Its thin wire melts when the current is too high, breaking the circuit
It makes the current flow faster
questions.explain: A fuse is a safety device that breaks the circuit before wires overheat.

questions.prompt: A 1150 W electric iron runs on 230 V. What current does it draw? (I = P ÷ V)
A 2000 W geyser runs for 30 minutes every day for 30 days. How many units (kWh) does it use?
In the Fuse Box, the geyser (2000 W) and induction cooktop (2000 W) were switched on together with a 15 A fuse. What happened, and why?
options: The fuse blew, because 4000 ÷ 230 ≈ 17 A, which is more than 15 A
questions.explain: Too much current overloads the circuit, so the fuse cuts it off.

questions.prompt: Someone suggests replacing a blown fuse wire with a thick copper wire ‘so it never blows again’. Explain why this is dangerous, and what should be done instead.
questions.modelAnswer: A thick copper wire won't melt even when the current is dangerously high. During an overload or short circuit, the house wiring could overheat and cause a fire, or appliances could be damaged. Instead, find and fix the cause (too many appliances or a faulty one), then replace the fuse with one of the correct rating, or install an MCB that trips and can be reset safely.
rubric: Thick wire won't melt at high current
Correct action: fix the cause and use the right rating or an MCB
questions.explain: Criterion D: evaluate a dangerous shortcut.

questions.text: When current flows through a wire, the wire gets ___. This is called the ___ effect of current.
questions.explain: All wires heat up a little; high-resistance wires heat up a lot.
